Commands:
  kvx [serve] [--reuse] [--setting=value…]
      serve vaults (the default with no command); with --reuse, use the kvx already serving this
      store, and serve when it stops
  kvx run [--setting=value… --] <app> [args…]
      run an app with kvx as its managed identity
  kvx env [--shell posix|fish|pwsh]
      print the same environment for your shell or IDE
  kvx import --vault <name> [--project <dir> | --id <user-secrets-id> | --file <secrets.json>] [--remove-plaintext]
      move .NET user-secrets into a vault
  kvx principal set --tenant <id> --client-id <id> [--for <id>]… [--default]
  kvx principal show
  kvx principal clear --client-id <id>
      store, list or remove the service principals kvx signs in as; apps get one with
      AZURE_CLIENT_ID set to its id or a --for alias, and --default serves apps that name none with
      Kvx:Passthrough=ServicePrincipal; the secret is read from stdin
  kvx doctor [--setting=value…]
      check name resolution, the certificate, the key protector, the serving kvx and its principals,
      and say how to fix what is wrong
  kvx describe [--setting=value…]
      where kvx listens and what apps need, as JSON, for tools
  kvx help [<topic> | <command>]
      this list, a guide, or one command

Settings (any command): --urls=…, --Kvx:Domain=…, --Kvx:TokenFile=…, see appsettings.json next to kvx.

  kvx help passthrough   Choose how apps reach other Azure services

# Use kvx from an Aspire AppHost

```sh
dotnet pack src/Kvx.Aspire.Hosting -o ./artifacts
dotnet add path/to/AppHost package Kvx.Aspire.Hosting --source ./artifacts
```

```csharp
var secrets = builder.AddAzureKeyVault("secrets").RunAsKvx();
builder.AddProject<Projects.MyApp>("myapp").WithReference(secrets);
```

`RunAsKvx` changes only run mode. The vault stays Aspire's own Azure Key Vault resource, so the app keeps Aspire's Key Vault client integration unchanged, and publishing still provisions a real Key Vault. The local run needs no Azure subscription.

In run mode the AppHost shows kvx as a resource with its logs. If your kvx is already serving, the AppHost uses it, so secrets you imported are there; otherwise it starts kvx and stops it again with the AppHost. Every resource that references the vault waits for kvx, gets it as its managed identity the way `kvx run` sets that up, and trusts its certificate. What those resources get for other Azure services is the same as for any app run through kvx: [passthrough.md](passthrough.md), or `kvx help passthrough`.

The AppHost's `Kvx` configuration section sets `Command` (default `kvx`) and `Settings`, a list of settings passed to every kvx command, for example `["--Kvx:Domain=…"]`. They must match the kvx you run yourself if the AppHost is to reuse it. [samples/Kvx.Aspire.Sample](../samples/Kvx.Aspire.Sample) is a working AppHost.

Online: https://github.com/roobie/kvx/blob/6c6590b4eaea535e1b25d482e505a248656671d4/docs/aspire.md

# Get started: serve vaults and run an app against them

## Install

```sh
dotnet pack src/Kvx.Server -o ./artifacts
dotnet tool install --global kvx --add-source ./artifacts
```

Settings live in `appsettings.json` next to the installed tool. Any of them can be overridden per command, for example `--urls=…` or `--Kvx:Passthrough=`. Client commands must use the same `urls` and `Kvx:TokenFile` as the server they talk to.

## Serve

```sh
kvx                     # or: kvx serve
```

Vaults are served at `https://<vault>.dev.localhost:5381`, with the ASP.NET Core development certificate, which covers `*.dev.localhost`. Each vault name is just a host label; vaults appear the first time you write to them.

The certificate has to exist and be trusted once per machine:

- **Windows, macOS:** Visual Studio and Rider usually do this already; otherwise run `dotnet dev-certs https --trust`.
- **Linux:** run `dotnet dev-certs https --trust`. .NET apps then trust it. It warns that OpenSSL needs `SSL_CERT_DIR`; that only matters for non-.NET tools such as curl, and `kvx run` and `kvx env` set it for them.

kvx refuses to start without a certificate. To serve another domain, set `Kvx:Domain` and give Kestrel a certificate for `*.<domain>` under `Kestrel:Certificates:Default`.

Vault names have to resolve to loopback:

- **macOS, most Linux:** they already do. On a Linux without systemd-resolved, `kvx doctor` names the `myhostname` module to install.
- **Windows:** run this once in an elevated PowerShell:

  ```powershell
  Add-DnsClientNrptRule -Namespace '.localhost' -NameServers '127.0.0.1'
  ```

  Windows then asks kvx for every `*.localhost` name, and kvx answers them with loopback on `127.0.0.1:53` while it runs, so new vaults resolve without further setup. Set `Kvx:Dns` to `off` to turn the responder off.
- **Anywhere the above can't work** (port 53 held by another program, Group Policy NRPT rules, no admin rights): add a `127.0.0.1 <vault>.dev.localhost` line per vault to the hosts file (`/etc/hosts`, `%SystemRoot%\Syst
[truncated]

# Move .NET user-secrets into a vault

```sh
kvx import --vault myapp --project src/MyApp            # or --id <UserSecretsId>, or --file secrets.json
kvx import --vault myapp --project src/MyApp --remove-plaintext
```

Keys are stored under the names the Key Vault configuration provider maps back, so `ConnectionStrings:Db` becomes `ConnectionStrings--Db`, and the app reads the same keys after:

```csharp
builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(new Uri("https://myapp.dev.localhost:5381"), new DefaultAzureCredential());
```

kvx reports any key that cannot be a secret name, and keeps the plaintext file unless every key was imported. Re-running skips secrets that are already in the vault unchanged.

Online: https://github.com/roobie/kvx/blob/6c6590b4eaea535e1b25d482e505a248656671d4/docs/import.md

# Choose how apps reach other Azure services

An app pointed at kvx through `DefaultAzureCredential` gets *all* its Azure tokens through kvx. `DefaultAzureCredential` keeps using the first credential that works, so once the app has a token from kvx, every Azure client in that process (Storage, Service Bus, Cosmos DB, ARM, …) asks kvx for its token too. kvx answers Key Vault itself. `Kvx:Passthrough` decides what every other request gets:

| `Kvx:Passthrough` | Apps reach other Azure services as |
|---|---|
| `AzureCli`, `AzureDeveloperCli`, `VisualStudio`, `AzurePowerShell` (default: all four) | you, through your own login |
| empty | nothing: apps reach only Key Vault |
| `ServicePrincipal` | a service principal kvx holds |

Whatever the mode, an app that names its identity with `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` gets the principal kvx holds for that id; see [each app as its own principal](#each-app-as-its-own-principal).

Switching `Kvx:Passthrough` takes a restart of kvx.

## Your own login (the default)

- **You must be signed in** with `az login`, `azd auth login`, Visual Studio or `Connect-AzAccount`, in the session kvx runs in. Otherwise those calls fail with `AuthenticationFailedException`, and the message says to sign in.
- **The app acts as you, not as its managed identity.** It sees your role assignments, your default tenant and your subscriptions, so access that works locally may still fail in production, and the reverse.
- **Anything holding the session token can get your Azure tokens from kvx.** That is the same reach as running `az account get-access-token` yourself, since the token file is readable only by you.

## Off

Set `Kvx:Passthrough` to an empty string. Apps then reach only Key Vault through kvx, and any other Azure client gets an error saying passthrough is off.

## Pass through as a service principal

With `Kvx:Passthrough` set to `ServicePrincipal`, kvx gets tokens for other Azure services by signing in as a service principal, not as you. The app then sees that principal's role assignments, which you ca
[truncated]

# Find out why something does not work

```sh
kvx doctor
```

Run it first. It checks what kvx needs from the machine (vault names resolving to loopback, a valid and trusted certificate for them, the key protector, a serving kvx, and each stored service principal signing in) and says how to fix each problem, because those problems otherwise show up as SDK errors that don't name the cause. Give it the same settings as the kvx you serve, for example `kvx doctor --Kvx:Domain=…`.

Problems doctor cannot see from outside the app:

- **An Azure client other than Key Vault fails with `AuthenticationFailedException`.** With the default passthrough, sign in in the session kvx runs in (`az login`, `azd auth login`, Visual Studio or `Connect-AzAccount`). With passthrough off, other services are not reachable through kvx by design. See `kvx help passthrough`.
- **The error names a client id kvx holds no principal for.** The app's environment has `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` set. Store a principal for it, add `--for <id>` to the one that stands in for it, or unset it. See `kvx help passthrough`.
- **A principal signs in but the app is denied.** A new principal has no role assignments; give it the ones production's identity has.
- **curl or another non-.NET tool rejects the certificate on Linux.** OpenSSL needs `SSL_CERT_DIR`; start the tool with `kvx run`, or set it with `kvx env`.
- **The store cannot be read on Windows after a password reset.** An administrator resetting your password (rather than you changing it) makes DPAPI-protected data, and with it the store, unreadable.

Setting up the certificate and name resolution is in `kvx help get-started`.

Online: https://github.com/roobie/kvx/blob/6c6590b4eaea535e1b25d482e505a248656671d4/docs/troubleshoot.md
